title: Finding Water
summary: How to locate and collect water in various wilderness environments.

sections.heading: Step 1 — Read Environmental Indicators
sections.body: Look for signs of water in the landscape. Animal tracks often lead to water; follow converging trails downhill. Watch for flocks of birds circling low, or swarms of insects. Lush green vegetation in dry areas indicates groundwater is close to the surface.
sections.warning: Do not follow carnivore tracks exclusively, as they do not necessarily stay near water.
sections.image_description: Lush valley with animal footprints leading downhill

sections.heading: Step 2 — Collect Rainwater and Dew
sections.body: Rainwater is generally clean and safe. Suspend a clean tarp or plastic sheet with corners tied to trees, placing a stone in the center to create a funnel. Collect dew in the morning by dragging a clean cotton cloth or bandana through tall grass, then wringing it out into a container.
sections.warning: Avoid collecting rainwater from metallic or rusty surfaces, or roofs with asbestos/chemical coatings.
sections.image_description: Tarp suspended with a rock in the middle dripping water into a bucket

sections.heading: Step 3 — Build a Transpiration Bag
sections.body: Wrap a large, clear plastic bag over a leafy, non-toxic tree branch. Tie the bag opening tightly around the branch with string or tape to seal in moisture. As the leaves sweat (transpire) in the sun, water vapor condenses on the plastic and pools at the lowest point. Drain daily.
sections.warning: Ensure the plant is not poisonous (e.g., avoid oleander or eucalyptus) as toxins can contaminate the water.
sections.image_description: Clear plastic bag tied around a green tree branch with water pooling at bottom

sections.heading: Step 4 — Dig in Swales and Dry Beds
sections.body: In dry riverbeds, look for green patches or the outside bend of the river where water naturally cuts deepest. Dig a hole 1 to 2 feet deep. Water should begin to seep into the hole. Let the muddy water settle before scooping it out to purify.
sections.warning: Seep water must still be purified (boiled or chemically treated) before drinking.
sections.image_description: Person digging in dry sand bend with water seeping up

when_to_use: When lost or stranded in the wilderness without access to a municipal water supply.
do_not: Drink urine, saltwater, or blood (this increases dehydration)
Drink water from plants/cacti without positive identification
Eat snow directly (melt it first to avoid lowering core body temperature)
Rely solely on finding surface water in arid regions
